[element-release-date]
=== `<release-date>` Release-Date

An important date in the life of a standard, such as the date it was first published or the date it was reinstated. The attributes <<attribute-date-type,`@date-type`>> and <<attribute-std-type,`@std-type`>> should be used to specify what event the date names.

#### Usage/Remarks
#### Date Type Attribute

<<attribute-date-type,`@date-type`>> is used to name events in the publishing cycle of the standards document (not in the lifecycle of the standard). Thus date types include events such as “`published`”, “`editorial-change`”, or “`stabilized-maintenance`”.
#### Standard Type Attribute

A <<attribute-std-type,`@std-type`>> attribute is used to name events (standards document types) in the lifecycle of the standard, such as “`addenda`” (which creates a new product, with a new designation that typically adds to a previous dated designation) or “`amendment`” (which replaces a previously published dated standard and also adds to a previous dated designation).
The original publication of a standard will carry a <<attribute-date-type,`@date-type`>> of “`published`” and a <<attribute-std-type,`@std-type`>> attribute of “`new-standard`”:
[source,xml]
....
<release-date date-type="published"
     std-type="new-standard">
....
Later corrections, amendments, editions, and alternate language versions for a standard will all carry this same release date naming the original publication; but they will also carry additional <<element-release-date,`<release-date>`>> elements that name the different dates on which they are published and the different types of lifecycle events they represent.
#### Specific Use Attribute

By design, the <<element-release-date,`<release-date>`>> element _does not_ take an <<attribute-specific-use,`@specific-use`>> attribute. If a date does not fit neatly into the <<attribute-date-type,`@date-type`>> and <<attribute-std-type,`@std-type`>> attributes just described, then that date should be tagged as a <<element-meta-date,`<meta-date>`>> element.
##### Use in Place of <<element-pub-date,`<pub-date>`>>

In the original ISO STS Tag Set, the element <<element-pub-date,`<pub-date>`>> was used to record the date on which an international standard was first published. NISO JATS has its own journal-article-based definition and attributes for the element <<element-pub-date,`<pub-date>`>>. In order to avoid a conflict for organizations which have both journal articles and standards in a single data store, NISO STS Best Practice is to record the date on which a standard is published (as well as other significant dates) using the element <<element-release-date,`<release-date>`>> instead of the element <<element-pub-date,`<pub-date>`>>.
##### If Release Date is _Not_ Available

The <<element-release-date,`<release-date>`>> is an optional element, so if the release date is not available, the element can just be omitted. If the <<element-release-date,`<release-date>`>> is unknown (for whatever reason) the word “`unknown`” could also be used as the element content:
[source,xml]
....
<release-date>unknown</release-date>
....

#### Tagged Samples

#### Published date inside `<std-meta>`

[source,xml]
....
...
<std-meta>
 ...
 <doc-ref>...</doc-ref>
 <release-date 
   iso-8601-date="2014-12-01" 
   date-type="published" 
   std-type="new-standard">2014-12-01</release-date>
 <comm-ref>...</comm-ref>
 ...
</std-meta>
...
....
#### ISO-specific, published date inside `<iso-meta>`

[source,xml]
....
...
<iso-meta>
 ...
 <content-language>en</content-language>
 <std-ref type="undated">ISO 2560</std-ref>
 <std-ref type="dated">ISO 2560:2009</std-ref>
 <doc-ref>ISO 2560:2009(en)</doc-ref>
 <release-date iso-8601-date="2009-05-30" 
   date-type="published">2009-05-30</release-date>
 ...  
</iso-meta>
...
....
